highlights: The Emperor issued a New Year Rescript reaffirming the Meiji Charter Oath and explicitly renouncing the concept of imperial divinity.
SCAP issued landmark 4 January directives ordering the removal of militarists from public office and abolishing ultra-nationalistic political organizations.
The International Military Tribunal for the Far East was established by special proclamation, and its formal Charter was approved.
SCAP directed the Japanese Government to abrogate all laws permitting licensed prostitution and annul all contracts binding women to prostitution.
Allied authorities impounded 394 industrial plants, including 294 aircraft and arsenal facilities, as the initial step in interim reparations.
Nationwide protests and strikes erupted across Southern Korea opposing the Moscow Conference agreement on a four-power trusteeship.
The first war atrocity trials at Yokohama concluded, resulting in two death sentences and one life imprisonment sentence.
Bank of Japan note issue expanded to ¥56 billion as the government halted direct overdraft borrowing to curb inflation.
keywords: International Military Tribunal for the Far East

sections.summary: General summary of non-military activities in Japan and Korea for January 1946.
sections.title: Part I: General

sections.summary: SCAP established the International Military Tribunal for the Far East and the General Accounting Section, Sixth Army was deactivated with Eighth Army assuming control, and USAMGIK was formally established in Korea.
sections.title: Organization under SCAP

sections.summary: The 4 January purge directives prompted reorganization of the Shidehara Cabinet, the Emperor renounced divinity in his New Year rescript, licensed prostitution was abolished, national elections were scheduled, and initial war crimes trials concluded in Yokohama.
sections.title: Political Activities in Japan

sections.summary: Allied custody was established over 394 industrial plants for reparations, coal output rose 41 percent, Bank of Japan note issue reached ¥56 billion, and new capital levy and war-profit tax bills were drafted.
sections.title: Economic Activities in Japan

sections.summary: A Tokyo nutrition survey showed half of food was obtained through black markets, typhus was checked while smallpox spread, 143 textbooks were cleared of militaristic content, and professional educators were appointed to lead the Education Ministry.
sections.title: Social Activities in Japan

sections.summary: USAMGIK assumed direct control over local military government units, widespread anti-trusteeship demonstrations erupted, a Korean constabulary was formed, and emergency rice collection efforts struggled against hoarding.
sections.title: Civil Administration in Korea

sections.summary: Political activities, civil administration, public safety, legal matters, and war crimes in Japan.
sections.title: Part II: Political - Japan

sections.summary: SCAP's purge directives prompted a major reshuffle of the Shidehara Cabinet and local governments, the Emperor issued an Imperial Rescript denying divinity, Communist leader Sanzo Nozaka returned from exile, and Japan's administrative authority was limited to the four main islands.
sections.title: Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Authorities combated widespread black-market operations and lethal bootleg whiskey, abolished the Keihei-tai auxiliary police while rearming civil police with revolvers, interned former German Ambassador Stahmer, and instituted mandatory censorship screening for all motion pictures.
sections.title: Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: The Supreme Commander approved the Charter for the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, SCAP ordered the arrest of 171 war crimes suspects including Koki Hirota and Yosuke Matsuoka, and Yokohama military commissions handed down two death sentences.
sections.title: Legal and War Crimes

sections.summary: Economic activities, natural resources, industry, commerce, labor, and finance in Japan.
sections.title: Part III: Economic - Japan

sections.summary: Government rice collections lagged at only 20 percent of quotas due to rampant black markets, the Agricultural Association Law was amended toward democratization, and a fuel-oil link system was instituted to stimulate fish deliveries.
sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries

sections.summary: Severe shortages of charcoal and lumber hampered urban heating and reconstruction, while coal production rebounded 41 percent following increased rations for miners, and geological surveys evaluated domestic nonferrous metal, cement, and quarrying capacities.
sections.title: Forestry and Mining

sections.summary: Allied authorities took custody of 394 aircraft plants, arsenals, and laboratories for reparations, while acute coal shortages suppressed industrial output across iron, steel, chemicals, textiles, and motor vehicles despite ambitious new housing construction targets.
sections.title: Industry

sections.summary: Railroads struggled with neglected rolling stock while planning widespread electrification and fare increases, commercial shipping remained crippled at a quarter of prewar capacity, and electric power consumption rose sharply due to residential space heating.
sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities

sections.summary: Foreign trade operated strictly under SCAP direction, with imports arriving of U.S. Army surplus flour, diesel oil, and medicines, while initial exports of raw silk, coal, pitch, and mining timbers were dispatched to Korea, China, and Hong Kong.
sections.title: Imports and Exports

sections.summary: Labor unions expanded rapidly at two per day and planned a national federation, winning substantial wage increases to offset soaring living costs, while an official registration recorded 32.7 million employed and 3.3 million unemployed.
sections.title: Labor

sections.summary: International radio and telephone circuits were restored with the United States and Britain, signal facilities were overhauled to support occupational forces, and production goals were established for 2.1 million radio receivers despite critical vacuum tube shortages.
sections.title: Communications

sections.summary: Staple food collections lagged, leaving Hokkaido cities with as little as two days of reserves, while the government abandoned vegetable auctions to reimpose official price ceilings on perishable foods amid surging living costs.
sections.title: Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: The Bank of Japan's currency issue expanded to a record ¥56 billion, direct government overdraft borrowing was halted, commercial banks restricted credit to essential producers, and liquidation of closed colonial and Axis financial institutions proceeded.
sections.title: Money and Banking

sections.summary: SCAP ordered strict fiscal retrenchment and the abolition of the Special Account for War Expenses, draft capital levy and war profit tax laws were prepared, and 41 companies including Oji Paper were added to the restricted Zaibatsu schedule.
sections.title: Public Finance

sections.summary: Public health, welfare, education, religion, and information media in Japan.
sections.title: Part IV: Social - Japan

sections.summary: SCAP directed curbs on rural-to-urban migration, the Welfare Ministry estimated 8,000,000 people needed relief, smallpox outbreaks triggered a nationwide vaccination drive, and repatriation through January processed over 1.2 million returning Japanese and 720,000 outbound foreign nationals.
sections.title: Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: Professional educators were appointed to head the Ministry of Education, English translations were required for textbook screening, Shinto was severed from state control, and media campaigns promoted democratic ideals and explained SCAP's political purge.
sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression

sections.summary: Political, economic, and social activities under USAMGIK in Southern Korea.
sections.title: Part V: Korea

sections.summary: Intense political turmoil and strikes erupted across Southern Korea following the Moscow Agreement's trusteeship announcement, coalition talks between Right and Left stalled, USAMGIK established Special Judicial Officers, and recruitment began for the Korean Constabulary.
sections.title: Political Activities in Korea

sections.summary: Rampant rice hoarding persisted despite ceiling prices and incentive programs, foreign trade was placed under rigid licensing control, the Chosen Stock Exchange was dissolved, and severe coal shortages from Japan crippled southern Korean manufacturing.
sections.title: Economic Activities in Korea

sections.summary: Educational planning committees drafted democratic school programs, free civic newspapers achieved over one million circulation, procedures were established to recover cultural property taken by Japan, and emergency relief and disease control aided incoming northern refugees.
sections.title: Social Activities in Korea

summary: Summation No. 4 documents non-military activities in Japan and American-occupied Korea during January 1946, marking a pivotal phase of early postwar transformation. In Japan, the Occupation accelerated institutional democratization through the landmark 4 January purge directives, the Emperor’s New Year rescript renouncing divinity, the abolition of licensed prostitution, and preparations for national elections. Allied authorities promulgated the Charter for the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, completed initial war crimes trials in Yokohama, and impounded 394 industrial plants for reparations. Concurrently, Japan confronted severe socioeconomic distress: acute food shortages, rampant black markets, and an expanding Bank of Japan note issue, counterbalanced by surging labor unionization and recovering coal production. In Southern Korea, the formal establishment of USAMGIK was overshadowed by massive public unrest following the Moscow Conference trusteeship announcement, while severe coal shortages and rice hoarding paralyzed the economy. For historians, this summation provides extraordinary empirical baselines: complete tabulations of Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Yasuda, and Sumitomo corporate subsidiaries, 20-year trends in agricultural output, national employment census data, nationwide disease maps, and the structural reorganization of Japanese education and police administration.
